analysis.one_liner: Lets gig companies pay workers in stock instead of wages and blocks state laws treating gig workers as employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and died with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would do two things. First, it would override any state law that presumes gig workers are employees entitled to wage rates or benefits, locking in their independent-contractor status nationwide [S3]. Second, it would let companies give contractors—and, at the company's option, even the users of its platform—private company stock as part of their pay without the securities registration normally required, and would require annual inflation adjustments to that exemption cap [S3]. In practice, app-based companies could pay workers in illiquid company shares while remaining free of state minimum-wage, overtime, and benefit rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig-economy platforms benefit most: they could keep classifying workers as contractors (avoiding state wage and benefit mandates) and could substitute company stock for cash pay, with a federal securities exemption covering the offer. Some contractors who want equity stakes in the platforms they work for could gain access to shares they cannot get today [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig-platform companies like ride-share and delivery apps

how_it_helps.text: Extends the SEC's existing 'Rule 701' securities exemption—now limited to employee compensation—so companies can offer private-company stock to contractors without registering those securities with the SEC [S2] [S3].
Allows the company, at its own election, to include even the users of its platform in the definition of 'customers' who may receive these securities [S3].

Preempts any state law that creates a presumption that gig workers are employees for purposes of wage rates or benefits, keeping them outside state minimum-wage, overtime, and benefit mandates [S2] [S3].
Requires the SEC to adjust the exemption's dollar cap annually for inflation and bars the SEC from writing rules that would restrict access to equity compensation for employees or contractors [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gig workers who rely on state laws for minimum wage, overtime, or benefits would lose those protections where states have passed them. Workers paid in private company stock would bear the risk that the shares are illiquid or lose value, while giving up cash wages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gig workers and state wage-and-benefit laws

drawbacks.text: Preempting state employee-classification rules would strip gig workers of state wage-rate and benefit protections—the very thing states pass such laws to secure [S2] [S3].
Equity as pay shifts risk onto workers: shares in private startups can be hard to sell and can lose value, unlike cash wages [S3].
Preemption overrides state policy choices with a federal rule, removing states' ability to set their own standards for who counts as an employee [S3].
Good-faith counterpoint: many gig workers say they value contractor flexibility, and equity stakes could let them share in a platform's growth—benefits the bill is designed to deliver [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The equity-compensation part offers a real, if risky, benefit to a subset of contractors who want a stake in the platforms they work for. But the bill pairs it with a sweeping preemption of state worker-classification laws, and the trade is not balanced: a worker could be offered volatile private stock while losing the state-law wage and benefit floor that cash employment provides. The bill also does nothing to guarantee workers could ever sell those shares.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Financial Services and Education and Workforce committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-NC) introduced the bill on April 13, 2023 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and, in addition, the House Education and Workforce Committee [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place; the bill accumulated no cosponsors [S4] [S5].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers in states with employee-classification or wage-benefit protections are better off because the bill died, and gig platforms remain better off than they would have been under it—since it never passed, they keep the existing rules but gain nothing. The status quo also preserved state lawmakers' authority over worker classification.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State wage-law protections and gig workers kept intact

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no party-line split ever formed around it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would lock in contractor classification—overriding state laws that presume gig workers are employees—and let platforms substitute company stock for cash pay, shifting wage risk onto workers while cutting labor costs [S3].
The bill extends a securities-registration exemption to contractors and platform users and indexes its dollar cap to inflation, making it cheaper to pay workers in stock [S3].
A broader Rule 701 exemption means less SEC registration friction for equity-based compensation offers [S3].
